questions.question: What is the Composer in the Compose runtime?
options: A View subclass that hosts composables inside an Activity
The scheduler that decides on which thread each composable should run on
A Gradle task that turns composable functions into XML layouts
The object passed through composable calls that records the composition
questions.explanation: The compiler adds a Composer parameter to every composable, and the runtime uses it to record groups, remembered values and node changes while the function runs. ComposeView is the View host, and scheduling recomposition is the Recomposer's job, not the Composer's.

questions.question: A @Composable function can be called from an ordinary, non-composable Kotlin function as long as it runs on the main thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Composable calls need the Composer that only flows through other composable functions, so calling one from a normal function is a compile error regardless of thread. The main thread is irrelevant; the restriction comes from the calling context.

questions.question: During recomposition, how do changes reach the actual UI node tree?
options: Each emit call mutates the LayoutNode tree immediately as code runs
The runtime diffs a fresh copy of the whole tree against the old one
Changes are recorded, then applied to the tree via the Applier
Nodes are rebuilt from scratch on every frame and swapped in atomically
questions.explanation: Composition records a list of node operations (insert, remove, move, update) and, once composition succeeds, they are applied to the tree through the Applier. This keeps the tree from being seen half-updated and lets a failed or cancelled composition be thrown away. There is no full-tree virtual DOM diff.

questions.question: With the default ViewCompositionStrategy, when is a ComposeView's Composition disposed?
options: When the host Activity's onDestroy is called, and not before that
When the view is detached from its window, unless it is pooled
When the hosting Fragment's onDestroyView runs, in every case
Never automatically; you must call disposeComposition() yourself
questions.explanation: The default strategy disposes the composition when the view leaves the window, but defers it when the view is inside a pooling container like RecyclerView, until it is released from the pool. In Fragments, DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed is often a better fit, but it is not the default.

questions.question: Why should side effects go in effect APIs (SideEffect, LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect) rather than directly in a composable's body? Select all that apply.
options: A composition can be discarded before it is applied, so the effect would run for UI that never appears
The Composer throws an exception if a composable body writes to any variable
A composable body may run many times, for example on every animation frame
Effect APIs run their work only after the composition has been applied successfully
questions.explanation: Composable bodies can re-run often and their results may be thrown away, so effects in the body can fire too often or for UI that never shows. Effect APIs are tied to the composition being applied and to the call leaving the composition. The runtime does not ban writes in the body; it just can't make them safe.

questions.question: A value provided with staticCompositionLocalOf changes. What gets recomposed?
options: Only the composables that actually read the local's current value
Nothing, since static locals cannot change after first composition
Only the direct child of the CompositionLocalProvider call
The provider's whole content, whether or not it reads the local
questions.explanation: Static locals don't track who reads them, so a change invalidates everything inside the provider's content. compositionLocalOf tracks reads and recomposes only the readers, at the cost of that bookkeeping. Static is the right choice for values that almost never change, such as a context or theme object.

questions.question: The Compose runtime is not tied to Android UI: with a different Applier, the same runtime can manage other node trees, such as vector graphics or non-UI trees.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The runtime only knows about groups, slots and abstract nodes; the Applier decides what those nodes are. Compose UI uses LayoutNode, vector painters run their own composition over vector nodes, and libraries use the runtime for trees that have nothing to do with Android Views.

questions.question: LazyColumn composes its items during the measure pass, in separate compositions. Why do CompositionLocals provided above the LazyColumn still reach item content?
options: Item compositions are created with the parent's CompositionContext
Locals are global singletons, so every composition in the process sees the same values
LazyColumn copies each local's value into the item's parameters at compile time
Item content is composed inside the parent composition, so no separate composition exists
questions.explanation: Subcompositions are created with a parent CompositionContext (the same mechanism rememberCompositionContext exposes), which links them to the parent for CompositionLocals and invalidations. Locals are scoped to the tree, not global, and items really are separate compositions built at measure time.

questions.question: Which statements about a Composition are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every composable function call creates its own new Composition
Disposing it calls onDispose for its DisposableEffects and forgets its remembered values
It holds the slot table that stores the groups and state for its content
setContent on Android creates one whose parent context is a Recomposer
questions.explanation: A Composition owns a slot table and is created by entry points like setContent, with a Recomposer as its parent context that schedules recomposition. Disposing it removes everything, firing onDispose and forgetting remembered objects. A normal composable call adds groups to the current composition; it doesn't make a new one.

questions.question: A composable like Text returns Unit. How does it put something on screen?
options: It returns a View that the parent adds to its hierarchy
It draws pixels straight onto the window's Canvas while the function is running
It ends up calling a node-emitting function that records a layout node
It registers a callback that the Activity calls during onDraw
questions.explanation: Composables describe UI by emitting nodes: deep down, Layout calls a node-emitting function such as ComposeNode, which records a LayoutNode insert or update through the Composer and Applier. Drawing happens later in the draw phase, not while the composable runs, and no Views are returned.
